clue.text: As tired and itchy divers might reach what's needed

definitions.text: As tired and itchy divers might
definitions.meaning: weary divers surface (rise from the depths) and itchy ones need to relieve the itch, so both halves of the phrase are acted out literally
to meet the required standard, an idiom from boxers toeing the line drawn on the ground

explanation.surface: A whimsical picture of exhausted, itching divers somehow managing to meet a required standard.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to meet the expected standard, originally a boxer stepping up to the line marked in the ring.

clue.text: In paradise, all the best mammals

parts.note: Eden is the biblical garden of paradise
a farewell, like the informal British goodbye ta-ta

explanation.surface: Someone declares that in paradise every mammal is the finest of its kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All the best' reads as praise for the mammals, but it is a parting phrase, the British ta-ta.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the zoological order of toothless mammals such as anteaters, sloths and armadillos.

clue.text: Where digits may be present

definitions.meaning: fingers (digits) are located on the hand
available, here and ready when needed

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means available or close by, and literally fingers sit attached to a hand.

clue.text: Unravelling toilet paper, endless amount that keeps on going

indicators.note: something unravelling comes apart and loses its order, so the letters gathered here are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: with no ends means the word amount loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A roll of toilet paper unwinding seems to go on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' takes A and T off AMOUNT, leaving MOUN; 'Unravelling' then shuffles TOILET PAPER with MOUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Perpetual motion is a hypothetical machine or movement that runs forever without stopping or any energy input.

clue.text: AC/DC group split in two

parts.note: slang for bisexual, shortened to bi
a sect is a group sharing beliefs

explanation.surface: Fans read about the rock band AC/DC breaking up into two halves.
explanation.walkthrough: AC/DC looks like the rock band or electric current, but it is old slang for bisexual.
explanation.definitionFit: To bisect is to cut something into two equal parts, the verb matching the past-tense phrasing here.

clue.text: Amusing lady and sister holding brief chat on it for a second, say

parts.note: amusing means fun
a dame is a lady

indicators.note: holding puts one piece inside another, here the nun around the shortened chat

parts.note: a nun is a religious sister

indicators.note: cut short means the word for chat loses its last letter

parts.note: chat means talk
taken as written

explanation.surface: A funny woman and her sister keep chattering for just a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brief' cuts TALK to TAL, which NUN is 'holding' to make NTALUN; 'on it' adds IT at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The second is the SI base unit of time, so it is an example of a basic unit of measurement.

clue.text: Apple's company guidelines rewritten with out-of-date content

indicators.note: being the contents of something means sitting inside it
written out again in a new form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: out-of-date means old

explanation.surface: Apple's corporate rules have been redrafted to include old-fashioned material.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apple' suggests the tech firm, but it is the fruit; 'rewritten' gives GENDELICIOUS and 'content' sets the old-fashioned piece just after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Golden Delicious is a well-known yellow-skinned variety of apple.

clue.text: Nationality of executed PM?

indicators.note: executed suggests beheading, so the name loses its head, the first letter

parts.note: Benjamin Disraeli was a Victorian British prime minister

explanation.surface: A quiz asks the nationality of a prime minister who was put to death.
explanation.walkthrough: Executing by beheading removes the head, so DISRAELI loses its D.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Israel holds Israeli nationality.

clue.text: Problem in the air after it's gone off

indicators.note: off as in gone bad or out of order, so the remaining letters are jumbled
gone means these letters have been taken away from the phrase

parts.note: taken as written
it's gives the letters of it

explanation.surface: Something is wrong in the atmosphere once it has left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gone' removes I and T from IN THE AIR, leaving NHEAIR, which 'off' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A hernia is a medical problem where an organ pushes through the wall containing it.

clue.text: Disperse unsettled August shower

indicators.note: not settled means the letters are disturbed and rearranged

explanation.surface: A summer rain shower in August scatters and breaks up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shower' suggests rain; it is a shower of meteors.
explanation.definitionFit: The Perseids are a meteor shower that peaks every year in mid-August.

clue.text: Approval — mine's full of praise

indicators.note: being full of something means containing it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine; the 's is is
to laud is to praise

explanation.surface: Someone receiving approval says their mine is overflowing with compliments.
explanation.definitionFit: A plaudit is an expression of praise or approval, often in the plural.

clue.text: Bury old doctor by part of hospital?

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: An elderly doctor is buried beside a hospital wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads old doctor first, but 'by' only means next to, and the hospital department comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To entomb is to place a body in a tomb, that is, to bury it.

clue.text: Literary quote contradicted by part of Britain

definitions.text: Literary quote contradicted by part of Britain

parts.words: Literary quote contradicted by part of Britain
parts.note: John Donne's famous line seems refuted by the Isle of Man, a place whose name says that Man really is island land

explanation.surface: A famous quotation is disproved by a piece of British geography.
explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man is strictly a Crown dependency, not part of Britain, but it lies in the British Isles.
explanation.definitionFit: This is John Donne's meditation line saying no person stands alone, while the Isle of Man literally is island.

clue.text: One covering stories about old, old dramatist

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
jokes begin 'have you heard the one about...', so stories are ones
C is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: A single person writing up stories about the past describes an elderly playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'old, old' looks like a stutter: one gives O, the other describes the playwright as of an earlier era. 'covering' is a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Ionesco (1909-94) was a Romanian-French playwright of the Theatre of the Absurd.

clue.text: Terminate holidays, not eating or drinking

parts.note: leave is time off work, holidays
being off your food or drink means not consuming it

explanation.surface: Someone cuts a holiday short while fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: To stop doing something is to give it up, so the phrasal verb means to cease or end.

clue.text: Insight of a copper with teammates

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
the men making up a team

explanation.surface: A police officer shows sharp understanding while working with colleagues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' suggests a policeman; it is the metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Acumen is keen perception or shrewdness, a kind of sharp understanding.

clue.text: For example, folk commit to race ahead of this commemoration

parts.words: For example, folk commit to race ahead of this
parts.note: folk, commit to and race are words that each come before the answer to form familiar phrases

explanation.surface: Examples of people pledging to run ahead of a remembrance event.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer follows each of folk, commit to and race in a common phrase; 'in ... of' gives the remembrance sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in memory of a person commemorates them, so remembrance and commemoration overlap.

clue.text: Make-up one's mother, covering a blemish

indicators.note: covering puts one piece around the other, so the mother wraps the rest

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother
a scar is a blemish on the skin

explanation.surface: A mother applies make-up to hide a mark on her face.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is cosmetic make-up applied to darken and thicken eyelashes.

clue.text: Wipe out bad smell in a couple of sewers?

indicators.note: in means the smell sits inside the other piece

parts.note: the first two letters of sewers
pong is British slang for a bad smell

explanation.surface: Cleaning up a nasty stink in a pair of sewage drains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sewers' reads as drains, but here it is just the word, giving SE.
explanation.definitionFit: To sponge something is to wipe it clean with a sponge, so it serves as a verb for cleaning off.

clue.text: Trade centre stocking some wild animal

indicators.note: a shop stocking goods holds them, so one piece is placed inside

parts.note: a mart is a market, a trading centre

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A market stocks a few untamed creatures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' turns the four letters into MOSE before the market takes them in; 'animal' is the definition, not 'wild animal'.
explanation.definitionFit: A marmoset is a small South American monkey, so it is a specific animal.

clue.text: Begin to take shots over cheeky lad catching boundaries in Edgbaston

parts.note: O stands for over in cricket scoring

indicators.note: catching holds something inside, so the lad goes around the boundaries

parts.note: a pup is a cheeky young man

indicators.note: the boundaries of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A cricketer at Edgbaston starts hitting, and a cheeky fielder takes a catch at the boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgbaston is a Test cricket ground in Birmingham; boundaries, overs and catches all belong to cricket, but here 'boundaries' just takes E and N.
explanation.definitionFit: To open up is to start firing, as guns begin shooting at a target.

clue.text: Cliff, little lad, just follows rude song

indicators.note: follows places the piece for just after the piece for rude

parts.note: a scar is a steep rocky cliff

indicators.note: little means shortened, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a lad is a boy
rough means crude or rude
fair means just

explanation.surface: Cliff Richard, a young lad, performs a crude song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cliff' suggests the singer Cliff Richard, but it is a rocky cliff.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarborough Fair is a traditional English ballad, famously recorded by Simon and Garfunkel.
